nodes.title: persistentData address
nodes.summary: how an entry is addressed by its instance and key
notes: An entry is addressed by the pair `instance` + `key`, and `key` alone is half an address. `instance` is an add-on instance UUID, the value the `Configure Persistent Data` script step takes in its `instance` slot. The same key can exist under several instances with different values.

`instance` is optional on a write and on delete. Omitting it, or sending `""`, addresses the entry that belongs to no instance, which is what the script step writes with its instance slot blank. A describe must state it, and a listing treats omitted and `""` differently (`help persistentData read list`).
Both halves match without case, and the stored spelling is the first one written: writing `Licence` and then `licence` updates one entry that still reports `Licence`.

Two pairs that build the same name, such as `(x-y, z)` and `(x, y-z)`, are one entry: the one written first, which keeps its pair. A write or delete that reaches an entry this way answers `ok` with a warning naming the pair it is filed under.
`instance` and `key` share one 99-character budget, so a 36-character instance leaves 63 for the key.
Neither half may contain a control character (U+0000 to U+001F). Breaking either limit is refused as `invalid_name`, naming the key at fault and the position.
An entry has no `id` and cannot be renamed: a pair that builds a different name is a different entry.

nodes.title: privilegeSet access
nodes.summary: how the records, layouts, scripts and valueLists grants combine
notes: `records`, `layouts`, `scripts` and `valueLists` are the four axes. Each takes `access`, a preset; a `new...` entry (`newTables`, `newLayouts`, `newScripts`, `newValueLists`), the grant for items added later; and a list of per-item grants. A new privilege set has no access on any axis, and an axis left out stays that way.

`access` is a preset. It sets the axis default and clears every per-item grant, as choosing it in Manage Security does. It is refused beside a non-empty item list; an empty list is accepted, so a describe can be sent back as it reads. There is no "custom" to send: an axis reads as custom when any item has a grant of its own.

A preset also sets what depends on it. `records` "createEditDelete" and "createEdit" make every field modifiable, and "viewOnly" makes every field view-only. `layouts` "allModifiable" and "allViewOnly" make the records reached through every layout modifiable or view-only, within the record and field access. On `layouts`, `scripts` and `valueLists` it sets `allowCreation` too.

A `new...` entry ([Any New Table], [Any New Layout] and so on) is the grant for items created later. It takes no name, and `access` "default" is refused on it. Beside a preset, an entry at another level applies to items added later only; existing items keep the preset's level as grants of their own. So `scripts` {"access":"allNoAccess","newScripts":{"access":"modifiable"}} denies every existing script, lets scripts added later be modified, and reads back as a per-script list with no `access`. On `newLayouts`, `access` or `records` may be sent alone; the one left out keeps its level.

Record access is not field access, and layout access is not access to the layout's records. A table entry without `fields` takes its field access from `newTables`, and a layout entry without `records` takes its record access from `newLayouts`. On a new set both are no access, so send both. On update, an omitted `fields` or `records` keeps the value in effect.

An item with no grant of its own has no entry on a read. Sending `access` "default" for an item removes its grant so that it follows the `new...` entry; on a table entry it drops the whole override. Grants for scripts, value lists, layouts and fields that no longer exist are not reported; where only such grants remain, the axis reads with an empty list and no `access`, and sending that back changes nothing.

nodes.title: calculations
nodes.summary: how a formula is sent, the Approximate keys and contextKey, and the calc_* errors
notes: A formula is sent in one of two forms. A calculation object, `{"text": "...", "context": "..."}`, is how a field's formula slots and a privilege set's record-access formulas take one. `text` is the formula. `context` is the table occurrence its field references resolve against: a formula reads its fields through a position in the relationship graph, so text alone names fields nothing can resolve. A privilege set also spells `context` as `tableOccurrence`.

A bare string is how every other formula is sent: a custom function's `body`, a value list's `calculation`, a custom menu's calculations, a script step's calculations, and the `calculation` of `validate:calculation` and `evaluate:calculation`. It has no table context, so a field in it is named `Occurrence::Field`. On `validate:calculation` and `evaluate:calculation` an optional `context` key beside it names an occurrence to resolve bare field names from; omit it for none.

In the object form `text` and `context` are both required, and neither may be empty, except that a read can give `textApproximate` in place of `text` and `contextKey` in place of `context`, as below. A `text` of nothing but white space is empty: FileMaker keeps no formula for it. White space here is what FileMaker's calculation parser skips between tokens: the space, tab, line feed, carriage return, vertical tab and form feed, the no-break space (U+00A0), the ideographic space (U+3000), U+1680, U+180E, U+2000 to U+200B and U+205F. A formula of nothing but a comment is not empty, and a formula sent as a bare string follows the same rule.

Five slots take an empty formula and store it, as FileMaker Pro stores one, with a warning: a field's own `calculation`, its `autoEnter.calculation`, its `validation.calculation`, a privilege set's limited-access formula and a value list's `calculation`. Every other slot refuses it as `invalid_field`.

A line break in a formula is a CR (`\r`), not an LF (`\n`). The text is used as sent, and a `//` comment ends only at a CR, so an LF after one makes the rest of the formula part of the comment, silently and with no error.

A formula a read cannot render is reported under a key ending in `Approximate`: `textApproximate` in place of `text`, `calculationApproximate` in place of `calculation`, `bodyApproximate` in place of `body`, and `<key>Approximate` for a script step's calculation. A calculation stores opcodes and keys, never names, so a name that cannot be looked up here reads back as `<Function Missing>`, `<Field Missing>`, `<Table Missing>`, `<Private Function>` or `<No Access>`: a plug-in function with the plug-in not installed, a deleted field or occurrence, a name this account may not see. The text is then not a formula, so it is not offered under the key a write parses, and the name is not in the file and cannot be recovered here. Once the name resolves again, the same formula reads under the ordinary key.

On a write, an `Approximate` key means keep the formula already stored. A read fed back to an update keeps the formula and changes anything else about the member. It is refused as `invalid_field` where the slot stores no formula, so always on a create, and where the text is not what the slot stores. Send the ordinary key to replace the formula. A script step is accepted only where the same step is being rewritten, so its body claims the step by its `uuid` and `stepID`.

A formula stored against an occurrence since deleted, or pointed at another table, reads with `contextKey`, the id it still stores, in place of `context`. Sent back with the text as read, it keeps the formula, and it is refused where the slot does not store that text against that key. A field the formula named through that occurrence reads as `<Field Missing>`, under `textApproximate`. To replace the formula, send `text` with a `context` naming one of the table's occurrences. A create has no stored formula to keep: a field's create stores the slot with no formula and warns.

A formula FileMaker will not parse is refused under the name this CLI gives its error, and one with no name is `invalid_field`. `dbError` on the error holds FileMaker's number. `details[0]` carries `path`, a JSON pointer to the formula in the op, and, where FileMaker points at the text, the `token` it stopped at with `errorBegin` and `errorEnd`, counted in code points of the text sent. Both are left out when FileMaker gives no position.

The names are `field_missing` (102), a field that does not exist; `table_missing` (106), an occurrence that does not exist or a field on one not related to the context; `parse_error` (1200); `calc_too_few_params` (1201) and `calc_too_many_params` (1202); `calc_unexpected_end` (1203); `calc_unexpected_token` (1204), where a number, text constant, field name or `(` was expected; `calc_unterminated_comment` (1205) and `calc_unterminated_string` (1206); `calc_unbalanced_paren` (1207); `calc_unknown_function` (1208), an unknown function name or a missing operator before `(`; `calc_unknown_name` (1209); `calc_invalid_summarized_field_type` (1220); `calc_invalid_summarized_data_type` (1221); `calc_cannot_be_stored` (1222); `calc_unimplemented` (1223); `calc_undefined` (1224); `calc_function_not_supported` (1225); and `calc_plugin_not_loaded` (113).

nodes.title: forms
nodes.summary: what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

forms.notes: most name-like string keys also refuse the empty string. A string is Unicode text: a line holding bytes that are not UTF-8, or a `\u` escape naming one half of a UTF-16 surrogate pair without the other (`\ud800` alone, `\udc00` with no first half before it), is refused as `invalid_encoding` before any op on it runs, wherever the string is -- the op, a key, a value at any depth. A character past U+FFFF is sent as UTF-8 or as both halves of its pair (`\ud83d\ude00`); U+FFFD, U+FEFF and the noncharacters are kept as sent, except that a custom value list value and a persistent data value refuse U+FFFF, which FileMaker cannot store in either

forms.json: a JSON number with no fractional part
forms.notes: when the key accepts only part of the number line, the range is on its own row. A number written as digits alone, from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807, is read exactly; one with a fraction or an exponent (`1.0`, `1e2`), or past that range, is read as a `number` is (below), and a key that takes only whole numbers refuses that as `invalid_field`

forms.json: a JSON number, whole or fractional
forms.notes: read as a 64-bit double, and refused as `invalid_json` when a double cannot hold it at full precision: when its nearest double is infinite, or when it is not 0 and rounds to less than 2.2250738585072014e-308 in magnitude (a subnormal, or so small it would read as 0). So a number other than 0 must round to between 2.2250738585072014e-308 and 1.7976931348623157e308 in magnitude; 0 is accepted however it is written, `0e999999` included
the strings "true" and "false" are refused; a boolean is not quoted

its own keys are a page of their own: ask for the key by name and they are answered the same way this page's keys are. An object gives each key once: a key repeated in one object, at any depth, is refused as `invalid_json` rather than one of its values being used. Objects and arrays nest at most 1000 deep, the op's own object included, and a line nested deeper is refused as `invalid_json`

`array of string` on the row means the elements are strings; `array of enum` means each element is one of the values listed on the row, matched without regard to case. An array of objects has a page of its own, asked for by the key's name; an array whose elements are documented elsewhere carries a pointer to that page instead. Arrays and objects nest at most 1000 deep, the op's own object included, and a line nested deeper is refused as `invalid_json`

forms.json: a JSON string, from a fixed list of accepted values
forms.notes: the accepted values are on the key's own row, ahead of the sentence, and they are matched without regard to case

forms.json: a JSON string from a fixed list of accepted values, or a JSON number with no fractional part
forms.notes: the accepted names are on the key's own row and are matched without regard to case; any whole number inside the row's min and max is accepted too, named or not

`text` is the formula and `context` the table occurrence its field references resolve against. Both formula forms, the empty formula, and the `textApproximate` and `contextKey` spellings a read can give are on `filemaker help reference calculations`

forms.json: any JSON value -- a string, number, boolean, object, array or null
forms.notes: the value's own shape is part of what it says, so the key's sentence says which shape each use takes -- nothing about it is checked before the op reads it

send it or leave it out
send exactly one of the keys named; none, or two, is refused
at least one of the keys named must be sent; more than one is allowed

conditions.words: send at least one of `<a>`, `<b>` when `<key>` is `<value>`
conditions.json: send at least one of the keys named when the other key has that value, or whatever its value when it reads "is sent". Otherwise this rule asks for nothing
required when the other key has that value. "Is sent" in place of a value means required when the other key is present, whatever its value
required unless the other key has that value; if the other key is left out, this one is required
refused when the other key has that value; "is sent" means refused when the other key is present at all
refused unless the other key has that value; if the other key is left out, this one is refused
reported on a read; a write must either omit it or send back exactly the value a read gave, and any other value is refused. Never a way to change what is stored

filters.notes: matches the whole name, compared the way FileMaker compares names
matches the whole value, compared the way FileMaker compares names, with `*` standing for any run of characters and `?` for exactly one
matches the value as given, character for character
keeps the items whose own flag is that value
keeps the items whose value is that number
keeps the items whose value falls between the bounds, each included. Either bound may be left out to leave that end open; leaving out both is refused
keeps the items whose own rectangle overlaps the one you send, not only the ones inside it. All four members are required

filters.json: a string, or an array of strings
filters.notes: a pattern string, or an array of patterns, matched as `glob` does and ignoring case. An array keeps the items carrying a match for every pattern. Empty strings and empty arrays are refused

notes: Each key reads as its name, its form, its requiredness and a sentence. `--json` gives the requiredness as a short code beside the words. `<a>`, `<b>`, `<key>` and `<value>` in the Conditions below stand for the keys and the value a real row names.
A key may carry several rules, joined with `; `: "required when `type` is `calc`; refused unless `type` is `calc`" is required with that type and refused without it. Every rule listed has to hold.

A bracketed tag such as `[glob on name]` marks a key that narrows a listing rather than describing a thing to write. It says how the comparison is made and which part of each listed item is compared; an item that has no such part never matches. The first word of the tag is one of the Filters above.

`needs detail` in that tag means the part compared is only on a detailed read, so the filter is refused unless the read asks for detail too. `as text` means the part is text rather than a name, so only the case of A to Z is ignored. `as a display name` means a theme's display name, compared ignoring the case of every letter that has one while counting a decomposed accent or a fullwidth letter as a different character.

Names are compared the way FileMaker compares them, wherever this CLI matches one: an address, a filter, a search term, a collision check. Case is ignored for A to Z, accented or not, whether an accent arrives as part of its letter or after it, and a fullwidth letter matches its ordinary form: `élan`, `ÉLAN` and `E` followed by U+0301 and `lan` all name `Élan`, and `ＡＢＣ` names `ABC`. Other differences count: `ΣΟΦΌΣ` and `Σοφός`, `STRAẞE` and `Straße`, and `ｶ` and `カ` are two names each, and an accent, a space or a punctuation mark always counts. Two spellings a create refuses as `duplicate_name` are one name everywhere. A result gives the stored spelling of a table name, not the one you sent.
`?` in a pattern is one character as a reader sees it, an accented letter however it is encoded or an emoji however many bytes it takes: `?lan` matches `Élan` and `A?B` matches `A😀B`.
seeAlso: `filemaker help script steps forms` — the same question for a script step's keys, which carry their own forms and types

nodes.title: ids
nodes.summary: how a member is addressed by name or id, the not-found code, and how ids are assigned
notes: A request names a member by its name or by its `id`. Where a page says to send `name` or `id`, send exactly one: both is refused as `invalid_field` and neither as `missing_field`. A catalog whose members have no name takes another handle in the same way, such as `keyword`, `path` or `uuid`. The id is the one a listing or an earlier write reported.

An address that matches nothing is `<catalog>_not_found`, named for the catalog addressed: `table_not_found`, `valueList_not_found`. Read, update and delete all answer it. A name that is close to a real one comes back with the closest names as `suggestions`; an id comes back with none. A filter on a listing is not an address, so a filter that matches nothing is an empty listing and not a not-found.
Where two members may share a name, the address is `ambiguous` and nothing is changed: `details.candidates` lists them, and the `id` of one names it.

On create, `id` makes the member with that id instead of one FileMaker assigns; leaving it out lets FileMaker assign, which is what a request without the key does. The `id` row gives the range, which is the largest id FileMaker can hold for that catalog. An `id` outside it is `invalid_field`. An `id` already taken is `id_in_use`, and nothing is created: it never falls back to a generated id, which would hide that the reference it was meant to preserve has broken. A field's id is taken per table, so the same id in another table is not a collision.

FileMaker moves its id counter past an id you send and never back. Once the counter reaches the top of the range, a create without an `id` is `ids_exhausted` and nothing is created. A create that sends a free `id` in the range still works and takes nothing from the counter. A duplicate numbers its copy from the counter too, and is `ids_exhausted` when that would pass the top.

`ownerId` stamps the add-on that created a member, so everything one add-on made can be told apart. It is a UUID in either of two spellings, in either case: 32 hexadecimal digits with no separators, or the same digits grouped 8-4-4-4-12 by hyphens. Braces, and hyphens anywhere else, are refused as `invalid_field` before anything is created. A read reports it hyphen-grouped and in upper case, so compare a stamp read back with the one sent as UUIDs, not as strings.
A duplicate starts unowned whatever the original was, so `ownerId` on a duplicate stamps the copy.

nodes.title: search
nodes.summary: what every search reports: result shape, possible hits, match, and names held as text
notes: The kind is part of the question and is never inferred. `search:field` and `search:layout` on the same term are two searches, and a term naming both a field and a layout has two right answers. The kind also decides which scanners run: a variable search never opens a layout.

A kind that is not one of the nine is refused before anything is searched. `search:nosuch` and `search:` name no catalog and are `unknown_catalog`. `search:theme`, `search:relation` and the other catalogs that are no kind of thing to look for are `invalid_op`, which names the nine.

`resolution` says what `hits` holds. `resolved`: the term names what `targets` lists, and `hits` holds its uses. `ambiguous`: it names more than one object of the kind, `targets` lists them, `hits` is empty and nothing was scanned. `notFound`: it names nothing, `candidates` holds the near misses and nothing was scanned. `unavailable`: it names something in another file that could not be opened, so nothing was scanned and nothing is known about whether it exists; `coverage` names the file and why. `text`: `search:text` alone, which names no object, and `hits` holds where the string occurs. `search:text` resolves no names, so it only ever answers `text`. `search:variable` has no catalog to look in, so it reads the file and answers `resolved` or `notFound`.

A term that names nothing is a successful result: `status` is `ok`, `resolution` is `notFound` and the run exits 0. Branch on `resolution`, never on `status` alone and never on an empty `hits`, which a typo and a genuinely unused object both produce. An ambiguous term has no id form to break the tie; a more qualified spelling, such as `Table::Field`, narrows it.

Each hit carries its `catalog`, `container` and `containerId`, a `snippet`, and `confidence`, which is `exact` or `possible`. `total` and `countsByCatalog` count the hits. `coverage` is on every result, including one that searched everything, and is the half to read before concluding that nothing uses the target: it names each area that was skipped or only partly covered, and why. A short hit list that says nothing about its coverage is indistinguishable from an exhaustive one.

A step's field reference that a read reports as a raw key is counted under `danglingFieldReferences` when the field is gone from a file that opens, and under `unavailableFieldReferences` when the occurrence it goes through is based on a file that could not be opened, where nothing is known of the field. Either way the step still counts as a use of that occurrence and of its table, and no field hit is made from a key that holds no name.

A hit's address arrives twice. `slot` is the key and value pairs a write op addresses by (`step` 7, `option` `field`). `slotPath` is the same address for a person to read (`step[7].field`, or `body` where the key is the whole address). Use `slot`: `slotPath` is lossy where a name contains a dot.

`addressable` says the matching update op takes a key at this slot, not that this one reference can be patched on its own. A custom function's `body` is addressable, and writing it replaces the whole body rather than the mention the hit points at. `false` means the slot has no write path.
`inEffect: false` marks a reference FileMaker keeps but does not use: a disabled step, a formula whose switch is off, a startup layout with its checkbox cleared. It is absent from a live hit.

Possible hits are reported by default, each with a `reason`. They are references a file cannot resolve until it runs: a field set by calculated name, a layout chosen by expression, a script called by name, or a name handed to a function as text. `exactOnly` drops them, and `coverage` then records that they were suppressed, so the shorter answer cannot read as no uses.

`match` governs both halves of the query, resolving the term against the kind and matching text. `exact`, the default, finds the name written in full. `glob` takes `*` and `?`, with no escape, so a literal `*` cannot be matched. `contains` is a case-insensitive substring. Resolving the term compares names the way FileMaker does in all three modes, so `exact` finds `Élan` for `élan` as it does for `ÉLAN`; see `filemaker help reference forms`. As text, `exact` is a whole word, made of letters, digits, `_` and non-ASCII characters, so `TODO` is found in `TODO: fix` and `See TODO.` but not in `TODOS`, and text is matched ignoring the case of A to Z only.

`includeText` adds the other question to the structural one: the term matched as raw text wherever text is reachable, alongside the references that resolve to the target. Every hit the search makes without it is still there, and every hit it adds is `possible`, since a string in a calculation is not by itself a reference. Where a slot stores a name that does not reference the target, such as a layout's occurrence spelled like the value list searched for, the name comes back as text, never as a use. `search:text` asks the text question on its own and refuses `includeText`.
Only this file is read. A name another file holds as text, or any other use another file makes of this one, is not found: search that file as well.
Searches never write. No scanner opens a catalog for writing, and `--dry-run` does not change what the op does.

A search is the way to learn what a delete or a rename will touch. `delete:field` checks privilege-set calculations and the recalculation dependency graph and nothing else, so a field used in a script or on a layout deletes cleanly and leaves the reference dangling.

Names held as text are matched as possible hits. A name is held as text when it sits in one of these places: a formula handing it to a function that looks an object up by name, such as `GetField ( "T::Name" )`, `ValueListItems`, `ExecuteSQL` or `Evaluate`; an `fmp://` or WebDirect URL's `script` parameter; a Data API URL's layout or script; a web page's `FileMaker.PerformScript`; an Execute FileMaker Data API request; a step that computes the script, layout, table occurrence or field it uses, such as Perform Script, Go to Layout, Go to Related Record or New Window by calculated name, or Set Field by Name; the field File Options' `OnWindowTransaction` trigger names; and a label's or button's `<<Occurrence::Field>>` held as characters rather than as a merge field. A name the formula builds from pieces, or takes from a field or a variable, cannot be matched. A rename of a script, layout, occurrence, field, value list, table or custom function carries every reference stored by key and none of these, which is why a rename warns about them.

A formula that hands a function a name as text is read the way FileMaker reads a formula, in whichever formula holds it: a script step, a layout object, a field definition, a calculated value list, a custom function, a custom menu or a privilege set. The call may be spaced from its `(` like any other, and a call inside a string or a comment does not count. A name the formula writes in quotes among the call's arguments, or in a Let variable it hands the call, is a hit, so a name it writes for some other purpose is reported too. In a query `.` also separates names, so `c.Name` names the column `Name`, and a field may be named with its occurrence computed, as in `Get ( LayoutTableName ) & "::Status"`.

An Execute FileMaker Data API request names what it reads as text, and the step looks each name up in this file when it runs, so each is a possible hit: its `layouts` and `layout.response` name a layout, `tables` an occurrence, the keys of `fieldData`, of each `query` request and of each `portalData` row and a `sort` level's `fieldName` a field, and a `sort` level's `sortOrder` a value list. A request written as one quoted JSON object is read key by key, so a name it holds anywhere else is not counted. One the formula builds -- with `JSONSetElement`, say -- is a hit wherever the formula writes the name in quotes, with `.` also separating the names of a path such as `fieldData.Status`. A layout's or an occurrence's name is HTML-decoded before FileMaker looks it up -- `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` -- so `"A & B"` names the layout `A & B`.

A label's or a button's `<<Occurrence::Field>>` held as characters is a possible hit, at the object's `text`, never an exact one. A merge field is one only where its name resolved when the text was written; characters written before the field existed stay characters, shown as typed, and become a merge field only when the text is written again -- edited in FileMaker Pro, or sent again as the object's `text`. They are matched by the name they spell, so they answer to that name alone: a rename leaves them naming the old one.

nodes.title: tags
nodes.summary: how a tag list is written and read, and which tags FileMaker reserves
notes: A tag is any word. No list of accepted values exists and none is checked. Send each tag without the leading `#` the file stores it behind.

A tag may not be empty and may not contain a space or a `#`: the file stores the whole list as one string of space-separated `#tag` tokens and has no escape. Any of these is refused as `invalid_field`.
On create, `tags` stores the list. On update it replaces the whole list: `[]` clears it, and leaving `tags` out keeps it.
A read gives `tags` as one entry per tag, without the `#`, and leaves the key out when the member has no tags.

FileMaker's own marks live in the same list. A read never shows them and an update never removes them. A tag beginning `^FMI*`, `^FMI_`, `^FMI%`, `_FMI_`, `^WA*` or `^WA%` is refused as `invalid_field`, so a list read from one member can be sent to another.

nodes.title: themeCss
nodes.summary: how theme CSS differs from W3C CSS: no cascade, a closed vocabulary, look-alike syntax
notes: There is no cascade. A selector chain is not matched against objects -- its tokens are the address of one slot in a flat dictionary, keyed by (object type, component, state), and the declaration block is written straight into that slot. There is no specificity: nothing is compared against anything else. Write each selector chain once; a chain written twice is refused (`invalid_css`).

A stylesheet is checked before it is written. Anything FileMaker would drop in silence -- an unknown property, a color name, an unknown state or object type, a repeated selector -- refuses the whole write as `invalid_css` with the line and column, and nothing is stored. A value that is kept but suspect, such as a `px` length, arrives on `warnings`.

Selector grammar: `objectType[.class-or-component][:state]`, with a space as the only combinator (descendant). There is no `>`, `+`, `~`, `[attr]`, `:nth-*`, or `:not()`. A comma-separated list of selectors is allowed and applies one declaration block to every address in the list.

The trailing `.class` is read two ways, depending on how many tokens come before it. Two tokens -- `drop_down .icon` -- address that sub-part, checked against the component list below. One token with a class glued onto the object type -- `field.myStyle:normal` -- defines a custom style named 'myStyle' instead, and the sub-part is never checked. So `field.text:normal { color: #ff0000 }` defines a custom style named 'text' and leaves the field's own text alone, and the write warns of it. Write the two-token form whenever you mean a sub-part.

States, lowercase and run together with no separator -- 19 in all: normal, hover, pressed, focus, enabled, disabled, checked, indeterminate, focushover, checkedhover, checkedpressed, indeterminatehover, indeterminatepressed, loading, droptarget, checkedfocus, pressedfocus, placeholder, placeholderhover.

`:active` is accepted only as an alias of `:checked` (`:activehover` of `:checkedhover`), which is why shipped themes write `tab_control:active`. `:inactive` is not a state, even though FileMaker's theme inspector shows an 'Inactive' state, and is refused (`invalid_css`). There is no spelling for that state in CSS.
State fallback works the way you'd expect from CSS custom properties: a property left unset in any state other than `:normal` falls back to that same style's own `:normal` value.

Components -- the sub-part named after the class token -- are a closed list of 27: self, inner_border, text, icon, baseline, repeat_border, option_item, contents, tab, tab_inner_border, row, row_alt, status_bar, progress_bar, completed, panel, panel_inner_border, scrollbar_top_button, scrollbar_bottom_button, scrollbar_track, scrollbar_thumb, tab_header, unscrollable_contents, dot, dot_container, row_active, button_bar_divider.

Only 8 shorthand properties exist: padding, margin, border-color, border-style, border-width, border-radius, overflow, writing-mode. There is no `border`, `background`, or `font` shorthand -- write the longhands (border-top-width, border-top-color, background-color, background-image, font-family, font-size, font-weight, ...) individually. Reaching for a web shorthand that doesn't exist here is the single most likely mistake.

The default unit is `pt`, not `px`. A `px` value is accepted and kept as written -- `12px` reads back as `12px` -- but FileMaker reads it as the same number of points, so it comes with a warning to write `pt` instead. There is also a FileMaker-only `line` unit for sizes relative to a line of text, e.g. `1.2line`.

A color is written as `transparent`, `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb(...)` or `rgba(...)`, and in no other way. There are no color names: `red` is not a color here, and neither is `white`. Channels are `0`-`255` or percentages, and the alpha of `rgba` runs `0`-`1` and is a plain number: FileMaker reads `50%` there as 50, so an alpha written as a percentage is refused. A part outside its range is stored at the nearest end of it, as CSS draws it, and the write says so on `warnings`. A hex color must be exactly three or six digits -- a shorter one is refused outright rather than read, because FileMaker's own reader does not survive it.
Gradients use only the legacy syntax: `-webkit-gradient(linear, 25% 0%, 25% 100%, from(rgba(...)), to(rgba(...)), color-stop(0.5, rgba(...)))`. `linear-gradient(...)` is not understood.
No at-rules at all -- no @media, @import, @font-face, @keyframes.

Around 40 FileMaker-only `-fm-*` properties cover what a web font or background can't express, e.g. `-fm-icon` (a name from a closed icon set, such as `down-arrow` -- never a URL), `-fm-icon-color`, `-fm-use-body-current-row-style`, `-fm-tategaki` (CJK vertical text), `-fm-rotation`, `-fm-override-with-classic`.

notes: A folder is a start and end pair of members; only the start is listed. `type` is chosen on create and cannot be updated: delete and recreate to change it.

A formula in a step may name schema created earlier in the same batch.

nodes.title: script folder
nodes.summary: how a "/"-separated folder path is read
notes: A path runs from the top level, folder by folder, separated by "/"; "" is the top level. Repeated, leading and trailing "/" are ignored, so `/Plain/Sub`, `Plain/Sub/` and `Plain//Sub` all name `Plain` > `Sub`.
A folder must already exist: one that does not is `script_not_found`, naming the folder that was missing and the one it was looked for in, with suggestions as whole paths. A path is never created.

A path is `ambiguous` only when more than one chain of folders spells it whole, and `error.details` then lists the candidates: two sibling folders of one name that both carry the path to its end, or a name holding "/" beside a chain that spells the same path. A duplicated name partway along is not enough: `Box/Twin/Deep` reaches the `Deep` in one of two sibling `Twin`s when the other holds none.

A folder's name may not contain "/" when it is created, renamed or copied (`invalid_name`). FileMaker Pro allows it; a folder it named `A/B` keeps its name and is reached by the path a read reports for its members. A script's own name may contain "/".

nodes.summary: One member's full definition, including its projected body and its token

keys.summary: the script, folder or separator to describe, by name
the script to describe, by the id a listing reported
narrows a duplicated `name` to one kind; refused alongside `id`

notes: A name matching more than one member is `ambiguous`, with the candidates in `error.details`; `type` narrows a name shared by a script and a folder to one kind. A name matching only other kinds is `script_not_found`, with what it did match in `error.details.candidates`.

`body` is a lossless projection: it elaborates back into a byte-identical tree. What a step keeps for a choice that is not in effect -- the script a Perform Script picked From list while it performs one By name, the calculation of a Go to Record set to First -- is left out, as FileMaker leaves it out of what it runs, and a write that claims the same step keeps it; see `filemaker help script steps forms`. An empty script is `[]`, never null or "".
A script carries the `token` a step-level write requires; see `help script update token`. Folders and separators have no body and no token.

Every step carries a `uuid`, its durable handle: `update:script`'s `edits` accepts one in place of a step index. In a `body`, a step carrying the `uuid` and `stepID` of the step it replaces is that step, and keeps the options a body cannot restate (an `opaque` step's, a `<key>Approximate` formula) and any stamps an add-on left on it. A step without one is written new. A step in a file old enough never to have been re-saved by a FileMaker that stores them has none.

A block step carries its extent, `"block": {"role": "opener", "start": 3, "end": 11}`, on every `If`, `Else`, `Else If`, `Loop`, `End Loop`, `Open Transaction` and `Commit Transaction`. `start` and `end` are the inclusive indexes of the steps that open and close the block, the same from either end; `role` is `opener`, `branch` or `closer`. The body stays flat and `block` is read-only on a write. It is absent on a step with no block role, on a disabled block step, and `end` is absent on an unclosed `If`.

A step whose options this CLI cannot read is projected with `opaque: true` and `editable: false`. Its stored options survive a write of the body it appears in as long as the step keeps its `uuid`; sent without it they are lost, and `update:script` warns.

A calculation this run cannot render is reported under `<key>Approximate`, such as `valueApproximate` instead of `value`. A body read from such a script writes back unchanged: the stored formula is carried across. That holds only where the same step is rewritten, claimed by its `uuid` and `stepID`, with the text unchanged. A positional run such as `parameters` reports `null` at that position and the stored text at the same position of a parallel `parametersApproximate` array, accepted back under the same rule. See `filemaker help reference calculations` for how a formula is sent, the Approximate keys and contextKey, and the calc_* errors.

`problems` lists the steps FileMaker Pro's Check for Problems marks, as `[{"path":"/N","step":"..."}]` where `path` is a JSON Pointer into `body`. Those are steps whose stored field, layout, script or formula references no longer resolve, and steps that take a target field and name none, such as a Set Field or Cut that acts on the active field. It is `[]` when none are found. While the batch holds schema it has not committed, `problemsUnavailable` carries the reason instead and `problems` is absent: the check resolves against committed state and would flag a field this batch just created. Commit and read again for a verdict on the stored state. It also lists a Go to Related Record using "Use external table's layouts" whose `from` is in no other FileMaker file. It does not check value-list references or most table-occurrence references, so `[]` is not proof that every reference is good. A listing does not report it.
seeAlso: `filemaker help reference forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: search:script
nodes.summary: Reports what runs a script: other scripts, triggers, buttons and custom menus

keys.summary: the name of the object to find the uses of, as the file spells it
how the term is compared; omit it for an exact match
also match the term as raw text, beyond what resolves to the target
drop the possible hits and report only what resolved

notes: A script called by name is a possible hit. `Perform Script by Name` and the script parameter of an expression-driven call name their target as text, so they are reported with a reason rather than resolved -- and a script that is only ever called that way looks unused until the possible hits are read.

A script in another file is no use of this file's script of that name. A step, button or menu item that performs a script through a `dataSource` -- or calls back through a `callbackDataSource` -- names one of that file's scripts, so it is not counted here, and `includeText` reports it as text. A data source that is this file itself counts as this file. A script called by name is looked up in this file whatever `dataSource` the step stores, as FileMaker looks it up, unless the name it computes begins with a data source and `::`.

A script a formula's text runs by name is a possible hit, in whichever formula holds it -- an Open URL step's, a web viewer's, a field's or any other. An `fmp://` URL naming this file runs the script its `script` parameter names, read URL-decoded, and it may name the file through `$`, `~` or a host, in any case, with or without its extension, as written or URL-decoded. A web page the formula writes runs the script whose name it hands `FileMaker.PerformScript`, `FileMaker.PerformScriptWithOption` or `FileMaker.PerformScriptAsync`. A WebDirect URL naming this file, `/fmi/webd/<file>`, runs its first `script` parameter, the key matched exactly and the value form-decoded, so a `+` is a space there. A Data API URL naming this file runs the script its path names, `/layouts/<layout>/script/<script>`, and those its `script`, `script.prerequest` and `script.presort` parameters name. A URL naming another file is no use of this file's script, and neither is a name that only contains the script's. Where the formula builds the URL or the page's argument -- `"fmp://$/" & Get ( FileName ) & "?script=" & $name` -- a script it names in quotes anywhere is reported, as a name handed to a function is. An Execute FileMaker Data API request names no script: FileMaker refuses its `script` keys.
See `filemaker help reference search` for what every search reports and which names are held as text.

nodes.title: script steps
nodes.summary: the steps a script body may contain
notes: A `body` is an array of step objects, each carrying an integer `stepID`; `step`, the name, is optional. An empty array is an empty script.

A body is checked in full before anything is written, `--dry-run` included. An unknown step or an unresolvable name is reported with every other diagnostic in `error.details`, and nothing is created or changed.

A step FileMaker has retired is refused as `unsupported_step`, naming the step; its page here is marked `obsolete`. A script that already contains one still reads, and `update:script` with `edits` changes the rest of it without restating the retired step.

A step whose script lives in its `dataSource` -- Perform Script, Perform Script on Server and its `callbackDataSource`, Install OnTimer Script, Configure Region Monitor Script, Configure Local Notification, Configure NFC Reading, Execute URL -- names the current file or a FileMaker data source there. An ODBC or Claris Studio data source (`sourceType` `odbc` or `magnolia`) holds tables, not scripts, and is `unsupported_operation`. Re-Login signs in to the current file or a FileMaker data source and is refused the same way. Open File and Close File take an ODBC or Claris Studio data source.

An update judges only the steps it writes. A written step that restates the reference the step it replaces already holds -- the same step id, data source and script, sent with its `uuid` in a `body` or as an `edits` rewrite -- is written as it is, so a script whose data source was later switched to ODBC or Claris Studio still takes a rename, a move, `hidden` and edits to its other steps. Pointing such a step at another script there is refused.

FileMaker stores a calculation it cannot resolve as a string literal of the whole text and reports success: `Contacts::Emial` becomes the string "Contacts::Emial". Every calculation is read back, and one that comes back quoted that way is `calc_autoquoted`. Any other difference is FileMaker's own spelling and is kept: `0.5` as `.5`, `100.00` as `100`, `1e3` as `1.0E+3`, a function or field name in the case it was defined with, `;` between a function's parameters. A read reports that spelling. See `filemaker help reference calculations` for how a formula is sent, the Approximate keys and contextKey, and the calc_* errors.

A dry run that passes says the body is well formed, not that it is the script intended. Step identity, block balance, calculation syntax, every name that has to resolve and every choice with a named list of values are checked. Whether the step makes sense is not: no option is required and none excludes another, so a step with no target, no value or two contradictory targets is accepted and stored. The exception is a value FileMaker would store and never read -- Go to Related Record's `from` beside its `fromName`, Configure AI Account's `verifySslCertificates` true beside a provider other than `other`, AVPlayer Play's values for two sources with no `source` -- which is `step_option_not_applicable`. Read the script back to check it. See `filemaker help script steps forms`.

The roster is the steps FileMaker's step palette offers. A step FileMaker has retired is not listed and is refused on a write (`unsupported_step`), though its page is still here, marked `obsolete`. An id FileMaker files under no palette group is left out and still writable; the plug-in step is the one that matters. An id that is not a step at all is `unknown_step`.
The plug-in step is id 186 whatever the plug-in calls it, and it takes `plugin` (the four-byte plug-in id as eight hex digits), `externalID` and `parmTypes`. Sent without `plugin` it is refused.

nodes.title: exportOptions
nodes.summary: an Export Records step's output format and export order

keys.summary: the output file type. Picking one is what makes the step authorable: the format is stored in the step's own profile, not derived from the path
the stored four-character type code, for one none of the words above name -- an obsolete Excel export, or the four spaces a step with no output file stores. Round-trips verbatim
the rest of the profile as hex: the XML grammar and XSL source, the Excel worksheet name. Carried rather than decoded, and byte-identical on a round trip

how the output file's bytes are encoded. Which values a format actually offers differs -- XML is UTF-8 only, Excel UTF-16 only -- and 'default' is not offered by any dialog: it is what an unconfigured step stores
the stored character-set byte, for a value none of the words above name
whether the exported values carry the current layout's number, date and time formatting instead of their raw stored form

whether the first output row holds the field names. Reported only when the stored record carries the byte for it -- a step this build wrote does not, so its absence means 'not stored' rather than false
whether the output header uses a field's alias rather than its name. No dialog sets this and everything FileMaker writes has it on, so leaving it out gets what the dialog would have written
the exported columns, in output order. Array position IS the column order and is stored exactly as sent
the fields the export groups by, outermost first. Grouping is what makes a summary column mean anything, so a 'summarizeBy' without a matching entry here exports nothing useful
the stored field-names row, predefined flag and field delimiter

seeAlso: `filemaker help reference forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take
notes: An export order needs a field per column, by 'field' or 'fieldKey' -- never both, since one storage key spelled two ways has no rule for which spelling wins. The same goes for 'summarizeBy' with 'summarizeByKey', 'format' with 'formatRaw' and 'characterSet' with 'characterSetRaw': a read sends the name wherever it can and the raw form only where it cannot, so both together are refused whether or not they agree.

A name may itself hold `::`, so an 'Occurrence::Field' value is read at each of its `::` and names the field of the one reading whose occurrence holds a field of that name: `Invoices::Line::Total` is field `Line::Total` of `Invoices`, or field `Total` of an occurrence `Invoices::Line`. A value two readings fit is refused as `ambiguous`; send the field by its raw key instead, which is how a read reports such a field.

A column is held to Sort Records' level rules, refused as `invalid_step_option`: its 'repetition' and its 'summarizeByRepetition' each count from 1 up to their field's own repetitions, and only a summary field's column takes a 'summarizeBy'. 'fieldKey' and 'summarizeByKey' are how a read reports a reference it cannot name, so one naming nothing the file can reach is written as sent, but never with a third element below 1; one that does resolve is checked exactly as the field it names, its third element standing for the repetition.

A column identical to one the step already stores is written as it is, without those checks: a field can lose repetitions and a summary field can be retyped after the column was written, and the read reporting it has to write back. The step is the one the write replaces -- matched by 'uuid' and 'stepID' in a body, the addressed step in an edit, and the button's or menu item's own action -- so a step sent without its 'uuid', and every step of a create, is checked in full.

A grouping entry that names no field reads `[0, 0]`, and is stored in one of two forms that a read cannot tell apart: FileMaker's own empty entry, which its XML shows as reference id 0, and an entry whose reference is empty, shown as id -1. A `[0, 0]` sent back for a step that stores either keeps that one, and a new `[0, 0]` is stored as FileMaker's own, id 0.

An export order record that FileMaker stores without its trailing options -- several Pro-authored steps hold one -- is not read: such a step reports no 'fields', 'groupBy' or option keys at all, though FileMaker's XML lists the columns and group the record holds. A write that leaves 'fields' out keeps that record as it is.
Omitting exportOptions leaves whatever is stored alone. Send null to remove it.

whether the per-field settings are stored at all. Absent storage is not the same as every field being false: with it absent FileMaker re-derives the settings from the schema when the step runs. Left out, this follows whether any per-field key was sent

notes: A column with no target is still an entry: the mapping is positional, so dropping a blank one would move every later column onto the wrong field. It names no field to write to or match on.

'targetTable', 'importAction', 'characterSet' and each column's 'target' and 'action' have a raw counterpart -- 'targetTableKey', 'importActionRaw', 'characterSetRaw', 'targetKey', 'actionRaw' -- that a read sends only where it cannot name the value. nodes.title: sortOrder
nodes.summary: a Sort Records step's sort order: which fields, which direction, which value list

keys.summary: the sort levels, outermost first, innermost last. Array position IS the level order and is stored exactly as sent
Keep records in sorted order as data changes; false turns it off. A read always reports it; leaving it out takes the default, true
Sort blank records last, regardless of direction. A read always reports it; leaving it out takes the default, false

seeAlso: `filemaker help reference forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take
notes: A sort level needs a field, by 'field' or 'fieldKey' -- never both, since one storage key spelled two ways has no rule for which spelling wins. The same goes for 'orderBy' with 'orderByKey', 'valueList' with 'valueListKey' and 'locale' with 'localeRaw': a level sending both is refused, whether or not they agree.

'fieldKey', 'valueListKey' and 'orderByKey' are how a read reports a reference that no longer resolves, so one naming nothing the file can reach is written as sent -- but never with a third element below 1, which is no repetition of any field. One that does resolve is checked exactly as the name it resolves to, its third element standing for the level's 'repetition' or 'orderByRepetition'.

A name may itself hold `::`, so an 'Occurrence::Field' value is read at each of its `::` and names the field of the one reading whose occurrence holds a field of that name: `Invoices::Line::Total` is field `Line::Total` of `Invoices`, or field `Total` of an occurrence `Invoices::Line`. A value two readings fit is refused as `ambiguous`; send the field by its raw key instead, which is how a read reports such a field.

A level identical to one the step already stores is written as it is, without the repetition and summary-field checks: a field can lose repetitions and a summary field can be retyped after the level was written, and the read reporting it has to write back. The step is the one the write replaces -- matched by 'uuid' and 'stepID' in a body, the addressed step in an edit, and the button's or menu item's own action -- so a step sent without its 'uuid', and every step of a create, is checked in full.

nodes.title: fields
nodes.summary: one level of a Sort Records step's sort order

keys.summary: the field this level sorts on, as 'Occurrence::Field'

`[tableKey, fieldKey]` as the raw stored numbers, with the repetition as an optional third element -- how a level is read back once its field no longer resolves, or when its 'field' would read two ways. Round-trips: send it back unchanged and the level survives. A key that resolves is held to the field's own repetitions
which repetition of a repeating field this level sorts on, counting from 1 up to the field's own repetitions. 1 is the default and is never reported back
how this level sorts. 'valueList' needs valueList; the other three stand alone
the direction, for the two orders whose word does not already say it. Refused if order is 'ascending' or 'descending' -- sending both would let them disagree

the whole stored order byte, for a bit none of the keys above name. On a level with a value list, 'valueList' also names the custom-order bit (2) FileMaker Pro's Sort dialog stores, so such a level reads without 'orderRaw'. Sent beside the 'order' it needs, it must agree with that and with 'descending' where they overlap, and is then stored as given. A 'valueList' level sent without it keeps that bit as the same level already stores it, and a new level leaves it clear, which FileMaker sorts and displays the same way
the value list this level sorts by, by name. A level carrying one says order 'valueList'
the value list's raw stored key, for one that no longer resolves by name
a summary field whose value reorders this level's groups, as 'Occurrence::Field'; any other kind of field is refused. Leaving it out means the groups are not reordered

the raw `[tableKey, fieldKey]` pair of a summary field that no longer resolves, or whose 'orderBy' would read two ways, with its repetition as an optional third element. A key that resolves must name a summary field, and a repetition it has
which repetition of the summary field reorders the groups, counting from 1 up to the summary field's own repetitions
the language this level sorts by, as its English name (for example 'Spanish'). Leaving it out sorts by the field's own language
the stored language number, for a language whose name does not round-trip through this key
